@@137356702 <h> History suggests inequality ends in catastrophe . We need another path <p> There may never have been a group that had it so good as the Japanese plutocrats of the 1930s . In that era , the richest one percent of Japanese society captured twenty percent of national income -- a third more than the top earners in America command today . Within a decade , however , most of that bounty had vanished . Their share of national income collapsed by more than two-thirds ; the value of their estates fell by 98 percent . <p> What happened ? Total war , total defeat , and foreign occupation . Mass mobilization forced the state to intervene in industrial production , double income taxes , restrict dividends , and requisition merchant ships . Inflation and destruction obliterated much of the elite 's remaining wealth . Then the American occupiers finished the job -- dissolving family-owned conglomerates , organizing powerful labor unions , and imposing a 90 percent marginal property tax . In a deep irony of history , the wealth leveling policies they imposed on Japan were more radical @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ depose leaders in the Global South who attempted redistribution programs of their own . <p> The ultimate beneficiaries were ordinary Japanese people , who still reside in one of the more egalitarian economies in the developed world . But its path was paved with bloodshed : roughly ten percent of the country 's population killed , its cities firebombed and devastated by atomic explosions . <p> Japan 's experience is the poster child for historian Walter Scheidel 's thesis in The Great Leveler : that stable times invariably cause elites to accumulate wealth at the expense of ordinary people , and that historically , only cataclysmic shocks -- what he calls the Four Horsemen of Leveling : war , revolution , pandemics , and state failure -- have ever reversed that accumulation . And even these horsemen only achieve leveling when they are apocalyptic in scale , rupturing society with extraordinary levels of violence , suffering , and misery . <p> Scheidel 's research is extensive and authoritative . If his thesis is correct , its implications are daunting . As historian Roman Krznaric has written , " no historical @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ futile all well-intentioned efforts to transform society by peaceful means . It suggests that the only pathway to a transformed , life-affirming future -- an ecocivilization -- is a blood-soaked one , littered with bodies . <p> Is apocalypse , then , our only gateway to a better future ? Or are there alternative routes that might avert calamitous suffering ? To explore that question seriously , we first have to reckon with a dire possibility -- that we are not approaching collapse , but are already inside it . <p> No second chance <p> In 2018 , sustainability professor Jem Bendell published " Deep Adaptation : A Map for Navigating Climate Tragedy , " which was downloaded roughly a million times within a few years . Bendell broke academic taboos by predicting that " we face inevitable near-term societal collapse " and that communities need to prepare for civil unrest , lawlessness , and breakdown of normal life . As climate statistics have continued to worsen beyond most predicted parameters , his arguments have become an increasingly central part of serious conversations about our future . <p> For Bendell @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that civilizational breakdown at least creates the opening for something genuinely new . Inbuilt structures of the dominant system have , for decades , systematically resisted and shut down virtually all attempts at positive transformation . Collapse , in this view , presents an opportunity -- perhaps the only one available . <p> There is a certain cogency to this argument . But further analysis tarnishes even this silver lining . There is a profound difference between the collapse of historical civilizations and that of today 's world system . Previously , no matter how catastrophic it felt to those experiencing it , collapse was geographically bounded . People were closer to the land and could turn to farming , hunting , and gathering . They could rebuild from the ruins while geographically distant societies followed their own trajectories . <p> Today 's civilization is , in political scientist Thomas Homer-Dixon 's words , " a single , tightly coupled human social-ecological system of planetary scope . " Collapse in the modern era would almost certainly mean the disintegration of the entire global system -- shattering the elaborately interconnected latticework @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ shipping , technology , and communications that keep most people sheltered and fed . Like a colossal house of cards , it would most likely all come crashing down . In its wake , we should anticipate a holocaust beyond anything humanity has ever experienced : billions of deaths from starvation , violence , and disease . <p> It gets worse . Over the past five thousand years , humankind has already depleted the more easily accessible energy sources and raw materials on Earth . Even in the aftermath of civilizational carnage , it is unlikely that future generations could ever rebuild a society to an advanced level of technological sophistication . As astronomer Fred Hoyle observed , " with coal gone , oil gone , high-grade metallic ores gone , no species however competent can make the long climb from primitive conditions to high-level technology . This is a one-shot affair . " <p> The stakes could not be higher . If modern civilization collapses , the human race will likely persist -- but we might be condemning our descendants for time immemorial to lives bounded by the limitations @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ command the energy fodder of enslaved or indentured labor . <p> This is why there is an overriding moral imperative for those of us alive today , with any capacity to effect change , to find and advance an alternative path -- and to do so before the tipping point arrives . <p> The Adaptive Cycle : Where are we ? <p> From a systems perspective , human society is a particular instance of a larger category of complex , self-organized adaptive systems . Scientists have studied the process of change in such systems extensively , and their insights deserve our closest attention . <p> An interdisciplinary group of hundreds of scientists has spent decades developing what is known as the Adaptive Cycle model of change , which applies to all kinds of complex systems -- from cells to ecosystems -- and is equally applicable to human civilization . The Adaptive Cycle describes a life cycle of four phases that virtually every living system passes through . <p> It begins with a rapid growth phase , in which innovative strategies exploit new opportunities . Gradually , the system settles into @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a long time , in which the future seems predictable , but gradually the system becomes increasingly brittle and resistant to change . At some point , a tipping point triggers what is called the release phase -- think of lightning igniting a forest fire , or coral reef bleaching , or civilizational breakdown . Following the collapse , a period of chaos and uncertainty ensues . New opportunities for creativity emerge , which is why the final stage is called the renewal phase . In this period , small chance events can drastically shape the future . <p> The Adaptive Cycle model applies to virtually every complex , living system . <p> Applying this model to modern civilization , we might place our current era somewhere in the late conservation phase . Ever since colonialism established Western control over the rest of the world , the dominant worldview has generated an interdependent set of legal , financial , and cultural institutions , maintained by technologies and infrastructure that are mutually reinforcing . The increased connectivity of the modern era has further entrenched this system , imposing economic and cultural @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ making transformative change almost unthinkable . Through cultural hegemony -- explored in an earlier piece in this series -- the system 's dominant institutions deflect popular attention from its structural defects , while economic inequality insulates elites from the worst effects of the approaching release . <p> The glaring implication of the Adaptive Cycle model is that we may be sliding , with gathering momentum , toward that release phase . And yet the progression from conservation to release phases warrants more careful attention -- because it contains clues to a potential way out . <p> Far from equilibrium : The window in the chaos <p> When a system approaches a tipping point , even a small disturbance can have enormous consequences , catalyzing strongly reinforcing feedback effects that are difficult or impossible to reverse . Scientists who study complex systems prior to tipping points have identified certain distinctive phenomena that have significant implications for our present moment . <p> One is what researchers call " flickering " : conditions begin to fluctuate erratically , swinging from one extreme to another with increasing frequency . Flickering has been observed in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , in overexploited fish stocks , and in lakes shifting from a clear to a turbid state . Another signal is " critical slowing down " : when the system is disturbed , it takes increasingly longer to return to its former equilibrium . Eventually , that equilibrium is forever lost as the tipping point sends the whole system through a period of chaos -- until it reaches the renewal phase . <p> As our world swings from crisis to crisis , and previously reliable norms shatter with bewildering speed , this far-from-equilibrium state seems to accurately describe the current era . Political theorist Michael J. Albert , in his systems-informed exploration of this century 's possible futures , Navigating the Polycrisis , identifies this as a " far-from-equilibrium crisis " condition -- and he argues that outcomes will be contingent on the capacities of activists , intellectuals , and progressive policymakers to formulate compelling narratives that resonate with people during these crises , nudging them toward alternative worldviews . <p> And it is here -- in the deteriorating chaos of our time -- that the opportunity may exist to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Four Horsemen . <p> Reweaving the fabric <p> Consider an analogy . You own a rug , but you do n't like the pattern woven into it . Try as you might , the weave is so tightly braided that you can barely isolate a thread , never mind transform its design . Now imagine that , as in a magic fable , the rug begins to unweave itself spontaneously , loosening its knots and randomly releasing its assorted threads . All of a sudden , you have an opportunity to reweave the rug into a different pattern before it entirely unravels . <p> This corresponds to the potential that the current moment presents to us : to reweave society 's fabric even as it unravels from its own internal contradictions . <p> Can we re-weave society 's fabric before it 's too late ? <p> Change theorists Richard Heinberg and Asher Miller helpfully identify two typical stages of this unraveling prior to collapse : destabilization and breakdown . In the current era , different components of the world order and different regions are experiencing varying degrees of each . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , overwhelmed by the epistemic chaos of social media , might be characterized as undergoing breakdown . Meanwhile , ordinary people living in Haiti , Gaza , or Sudan are already suffering the full onslaught of collapse , while Indigenous peoples worldwide have endured for generations the aftermath of their own near-annihilation . Overall , we might anticipate a worldwide decades-long lurching decline in material and ethical standards , with some societies collapsing while others struggle on . <p> This bleak picture nevertheless opens up greater possibilities for a swerve toward an ecocivilization pathway . As the flickering worsens , new generations will increasingly recognize that the system is dying . Many will turn , as they 're already doing , to tribalism and authoritarianism . But as the coherence of the dominant civilization unravels , its cultural hegemony begins to lose its grip . Young people , rejecting the failed narratives of previous generations , are likely to become increasingly open to radically different alternatives -- alternatives that offer a life-enhancing future rather than an accelerating descent . <p> Crisis , movements , ideas : The disruption nexus <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ this critical juncture in a model he calls the Disruption Nexus . Rapid , transformative change occurs only when three elements are simultaneously in place and mutually reinforcing : crisis , movements , and ideas . <p> Crisis is required to destabilize the system from the equilibrium of its conservation phase . Powerful movements must arise , composed of large numbers of people alienated from the dominant system and willing to challenge those who hold power . And those movements must wield visionary ideas -- a coherent and radically alternative set of policies and practices from those that predominated in the old system . <p> At the moment , we have crisis in abundance . Movements have emerged -- Occupy , Black Lives Matter , the climate justice movement -- but they have not yet achieved the fervent worldwide adoption with staying power that civilizational transformation requires . And while alternative ideas already exist ( as I 've tried to lay out comprehensively in Ecocivilization ) , the work of weaving them into a coherent fabric , capable of inspiring mass adoption across many cultures and constituencies , remains largely @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ unravels , through a deft intertwining of movements and ideas , defines the challenge facing all those who desire a better future . The psychic distress caused by social breakdown frequently engenders feelings of panic , fear , and rage -- which can lead people further into the sway of authoritarian strongmen who fuel those very emotions . There is no guarantee of success . The window is open , but it will not stay open indefinitely . <p> Difficult as this task is -- and it may be the most difficult task our species has ever faced -- it is the calling that our times demand . <p> In my next couple of pieces , I 'll explore what it actually looks like to answer that calling : the specific strategies , at different scales , that might allow this unraveling and reweaving to become something more than metaphor . <h> Support Countercurrents <p> Countercurrents.org is on annual fundraising drive . @@137390089 <h> When They Call You Cockroach <p> Rwandan President , Juv ? nal Habyarimana 's plane was shot down over the sky of capital Kigali on the night of April 6 , 1994 . Immediately after his death , Radio Mille Collines was giving instructions and announced that the Tutsi ( minority ethnic group of Rwanda ) were inyenzi or Cockroaches . The massacre started soon at dawn . <p> Language did n't cause of the Rwandan genocide . It made , however , the ground . Scholars of genocide have explained that dehumanization is an integral and intentional element of extermination . You ca n't recruit ordinary people to go and kill fellow neighbor and human being , with whom you may have shared meals or worked without first dehumanizing them . That 's what the cockroach does . It 's more than an insult . It 's a permit . <p> This is worth noticing when political leaders and top constitutional figures in today 's democracies use the similar words . It 's not a diagnosis of genocidal intent , but a question over what such language empowers @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ not new . It has consistent history from the time of colonization . Colonized peoples characterized by colonial rulers as animal-like , ungovernable , teeming . German Nazis created a whole bureaucratic apparatus of pest-language . Jews were called as rats , carriers of disease . Gaza is another case study . Where Israel 's Defence Minister Yoav Gallant described Palestinians as " human animals " The local grammar was used in each time . But the logic is same . Anyone who exists outside the dominant social contract and dominant moral universe is called ' Vermin ' . <p> Commentators debated over Donald Trump comment in 2018 , when he said migrants were " infesting " America . They debated whether it is actually a calculated move or simply an unconsidered phrase . This debate missed the point . The word ' Infest ' is not a policy phrase . It is the term used to refer to a biological invasion . It demands its own extermination in its essence . Once the speaker says it , it does its job on its own . <p> In the recent @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to refer Bangladeshi migrants closer to home , in 2019 . This did n't come from a fringe activist ! A senior minister of the country used it in regard to then proposed citizenship law . Just like cockroaches , termites are also pests to eradicate . They have no history , no family , no grievances , or rights . This is the meaning of the metaphor . <p> The use of this jargon becomes particularly problematic when it is used by the very high executive . It 's creating the structure of exclusion . When a state 's spokesperson classifies any demographic group as infestation , this sends a clear message to the entire apparatus of the state , both formal and informal , who is worthy of protection . Be it Police discretion , judicial interpretation , administrative procedure or neighborhood vigilantism , all of it takes its cue from the moral register that power establishes . The word permeates and becomes a reality . <p> Ambedkar knew this . He continually and persistently revisited the idea of fraternity in his writing and speeches . Fraternity was @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ was a structural necessity . he argued , if fraternity is lacking , liberty and equality became a formality and it secures no one . He was writing in opposition to a social system that for centuries had deemed some people polluting , untouchable , less than fully human . He knew that the constitution would not only be one that gave citizens their rights , but one that helped to establish a new moral system where each human being 's right to dignity could never be taken away . <p> But these dehumanizing pest-language directly dismantle the very constitutional architecture . It does not involve the debate on rights . It preempts them . <p> The important factor is to see , how these terminologies are almost never used against the economically powerful and dominant majoritarian caste and class . It does n't refer to industrialists who pollute rivers or contractors who violets labor law . It 's for those who are already defined by their mere presence as transgressing : migrants , minorities , dissenters and the poor . The cockroach-metaphor works as a caste or as a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> The constitutional moment in India was grounded on the radical notion that the expendability was not a natural feature of certain bodies but a political choice that democracy was supposed to rule out . That 's the hope of the Preamble . <p> When this mode of language becomes part of the mainstream political debates and bureaucratic language and not seriously contested by any of the institutions , what we are seeing as the acceptance of hierarchy which the constitution explicitly refuted . It 's not sudden . It 's incremental . What can be said can be thought and what can be thought can be done . This is how a moral low is achieved . <p> The cockroach is no different ! It was employed in all political systems and in each of them it left a record . It 's not an overreaction to read that record carefully . This is the minimum seriousness that a democracy demands . <h> Subscribe to Our Newsletter <p> Himadri Sekhar Mistri is a researcher at the Centre for the Study of Social Systems , Jawaharlal Nehru University , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ violence , social movements and contemporary democracies . <p> Organised anti-immigration demonstrations have swept through South African cities in recent weeks . @@137409005 <h> How Kamala Harris sank : Democrats admit 2024 went horribly wrong but have no roadmap for 2028 <p> TOI correspondent from Washington : After months of secrecy , recrimination , leaks , and intra-party paranoia , the Democratic Party on Thursday released its long-awaited autopsy of the disastrous 2024 presidential campaign that resulted in Kamala Harris losing the election to Donald Trump , turning the post mortem into another debacle . The 192-page review , authored principally by Democratic strategist Paul Rivera , was intended to explain how Kamala Harris lost the 2024 election to Trump despite massive fundraising , a late burst of enthusiasm after President Joe Biden exited the race , and widespread Democratic warnings that the MAGA supremo represented an existential threat to American democracy . Instead , the report has exposed a party still deeply divided over what exactly went wrong.The report paints a picture of a Democratic Party disconnected from working-class voters , weak on economic messaging , culturally overextended , and organizationally complacent . It argues Democrats lost credibility on immigration , public safety , and inflation while Republicans successfully portrayed Harris as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ most striking is not what the autopsy says , but what it awkwardly avoids saying . <p> The report notably sidesteps a sustained examination of Biden 's disastrous decision to seek re-election despite widespread voter concerns about his age and stamina -- concerns Democrats publicly dismissed until his catastrophic debate performance forced his withdrawal . Nor does it seriously scrutinize the chaotic process that elevated Harris to the nomination without a competitive primary after Biden stepped aside in July 2024 . That omission has enraged many Democrats who believe the party establishment is still protecting senior figures like Nancy Pelosi and Chuck Schumer from accountability.The report also barely touches another politically explosive issue : divisions within the party over U.S. support for Israel 's war in Gaza , a conflict that alienated many younger and progressive voters . Critics immediately noted that a nearly 200-page document about Democratic collapse managed to avoid even mentioning " Gaza " or " Palestine " in any meaningful way.The findings themselves often read less like a dramatic revelation than a compilation of painful truths Democrats have spent two years arguing about on podcasts , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ report concludes , failed to connect with Latino voters , men , rural Americans and younger voters . The party remained too dependent on traditional media and too detached from emerging digital ecosystems dominated by MAGA Republicans . Trump 's campaign , it says , learned more from Barack Obama 's 2008 organizing revolution than Dems did.The autopsy also criticizes Democratic spending practices , suggesting the Harris campaign burned through astonishing sums of money with questionable efficiency . Harris raised roughly $1 billion in a compressed 107-day campaign but still failed to overcome voter dissatisfaction with the economy , immigration , and perceptions of elite detachment.But the most extraordinary feature of the release is the Democratic National Committee 's own disclaimer attached to the document . DNC chairman Ken Martin practically disowned the report while publishing it , while acknowledging the document was incomplete , unpolished and lacking adequate sourcing . " I am not proud of this product , " he admitted , while emphasizing that transparency required its release anyway.The debacle captures the Democratic Party 's broader predicament heading into 2028 . On one side are establishment figures @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ against an increasingly unpopular Trump administration . On the other are progressives and younger activists who believe the party suffers from something deeper : a leadership culture that is risk-averse , consultant-driven , overly managerial , and terrified of genuine ideological conflict.Many Dems privately concede Harris faced nearly impossible circumstances after inheriting the nomination late . The result was a campaign that often appeared caught between defending Biden 's record and promising generational change -- an impossible political yoga pose.For now , Democrats are trying to focus on the 2026 midterms , where Trump 's polarizing presidency may once again help unify the anti-Republican vote . But the autopsy suggests the party still has no settled answer to the larger question haunting it since 2024 : whether Trump 's victory was an aberration -- or evidence that Democrats have fundamentally lost touch with large sections of the American electorate .

@@137506791 <h> Iran Holds the Upper Edge ? A Strategic and Political Assessment <p> Iran maintains a surprising strategic advantage due to its asymmetric capabilities and geographic positioning . By effectively militarizing the Strait of Hormuz -- the vital maritime route for Persian Gulf oil and gas -- and expanding hostilities , Tehran has thwarted a decisive U.S. and Israeli victory , using regional leverage to force Washington to negotiate concessions . <p> The dominant Western narrative still presents Israel as militarily superior and Iran as cornered . But wars are not won only by superior airpower or spectacular strikes . They are won politically , economically , psychologically , and through endurance . In that broader sense , Iran appears to have gained significant leverage in this confrontation . <p> What is increasingly visible is the emergence of a new geopolitical reality : the decline of unquestioned American-Israeli dominance in West Asia . Analysts now openly discuss a shifting world order where U.S. coercive power no longer guarantees political victory . <p> Iran does not need to defeat Israel conventionally . It only needs to survive , sustain pressure , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ confrontation continues , the greater the political and economic burden on Israel and the United States . Iran is executing an asymmetrical war of endurance against Israel and the United States . By utilizing proxy networks and strategic friction , Tehran aims to survive conventional military pressure while escalating the political and economic costs of the conflict . <p> The primary components of this long-term strategy include the cost-exchange ratio . Iran forces Israel and the United States to expend highly expensive , multi-million-dollar interceptors ( like the Arrow and Iron Dome systems ) to destroy relatively low-cost , mass-produced drones and missiles . <p> By threatening maritime corridors and energy infrastructure , Iran drives up global shipping , insurance , and energy costs . This financial bleed is intended to outlast the Israeli and U.S. willingness to fund a protracted , multi-front conflict thus inviting economic attrition on the enemy . Sustained warfare inherently strains domestic economies , political cohesion , and reserve military forces in allied nations . Tehran calculates that the cumulative political burden will eventually force a compromise in their favour . <p> The Strait of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Iran 's favour.Iran 's geographical control over one of the world 's most critical oil corridors gives it enormous leverage . Disruption there affects global fuel prices , shipping , inflation , and Western economies . <p> Israel 's dependence on the United States paints a bleak picture of Israel 's boastful strength . Pentagon assessments reportedly show the United States carrying much of Israel 's missile-defense burden , depleting advanced interceptor stockpiles . This raises questions about sustainability and strategic overstretch . <p> The war also lacks political legitimacy in the Global South . Across much of Asia , Africa , and Latin America , the war is increasingly viewed not as " defense of democracy " but as another episode of Western military intervention and regional domination . <p> Above all , USA 's much trumpeted failure of regime-change ambitions gives Iran a psychological advantage and morale boost.Despite heavy strikes , Iran 's state structure remains intact . There is no evidence of collapse , surrender , or abandonment of strategic goals . <p> At the same time , caution is necessary . Israel retains devastating military capabilities @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ military and infrastructural damage . Civilian casualties on all sides remain morally indefensible . <p> But history repeatedly shows that technologically superior powers often fail against nations prepared for prolonged resistance . Vietnam , Iraq , Afghanistan , Lebanon in 2006 -- all exposed the limits of overwhelming force when political legitimacy erodes . <p> The war between Iran and Israel is no longer merely a regional confrontation . It has become a defining test of the emerging global order . Beneath the missiles , airstrikes , and diplomatic threats lies a larger struggle over power itself : Who controls the political future of West Asia ? Can the United States still dictate outcomes through force ? And is Israel 's long-standing military dominance beginning to encounter structural limits ? <p> Contrary to much Western media framing , Iran may today hold the strategic upper edge -- not necessarily because it is militarily stronger in conventional terms , but because it has succeeded in transforming the conflict into a war of endurance , legitimacy , and geopolitical cost . <p> Yet months into the conflict , Israel and the United @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ state apparatus remains functional . Its missile capability , though degraded , remains operational . Regional allies continue to exert pressure across multiple fronts . Most importantly , Iran has demonstrated an ability to absorb punishment while steadily raising the cost of continued war . <p> That changes the strategic equation . <p> Military superiority alone does not determine victory . The United States possessed overwhelming military superiority in Vietnam , Iraq , and Afghanistan . Yet each war revealed a fundamental truth : modern wars are ultimately political contests . A state that can survive , resist , and impose long-term costs can often outlast materially stronger opponents . Iran appears to understand this reality far better than Washington or Tel Aviv . <p> One of Iran 's greatest advantages is geography . The Strait of Hormuz remains one of the most important energy chokepoints on earth . Roughly one-fifth of global oil flows through it . Iran 's ability to threaten or partially disrupt that corridor gives it leverage far beyond its conventional military strength . <p> Oil markets react not merely to actual disruption but to fear @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with analysts warning that even if the war ended immediately , global energy markets could remain unstable for months or years . <p> This matters politically . Wars become difficult to sustain when ordinary citizens begin paying economic costs . Inflation , fuel prices , shipping disruptions , and military expenditures create domestic pressure in Western countries . Democracies may wage wars abroad , but they can not easily escape public exhaustion at home . <p> Meanwhile , reports suggest that the United States has borne the overwhelming burden of defending Israel from missile attacks , using significant portions of its advanced interceptor inventory . This reveals another uncomfortable reality : Israel 's security architecture remains heavily dependent on American logistical and military support . <p> The longer the war drags on , the more visible this dependence becomes . <p> At the geopolitical level , the conflict is accelerating the decline of the unipolar world . For decades after the Cold War , the United States operated as the uncontested global power . Military intervention , sanctions , regime-change operations , and economic coercion became normalized instruments of policy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ China increasingly challenge Western influence . Regional powers like T ? rkiye and Saudi Arabia pursue more independent policies . Much of the Global South views American foreign policy with growing scepticism , especially after Iraq , Libya , Gaza , and now Iran . <p> Indeed , many countries no longer see Western military intervention as morally credible . Instead , they increasingly interpret such wars through the lens of power politics , double standards , and imperial overreach . <p> This perception benefits Iran politically . <p> Iran has positioned itself -- not always convincingly , but effectively enough for many audiences -- as a state resisting Western domination . Whether one agrees with Iran 's internal politics is secondary to the broader symbolic reality : much of the non-Western world sees Iran standing against a heavily armed alliance backed by the world 's strongest military power . <p> That symbolism matters . <p> Israel , meanwhile , faces a deepening legitimacy crisis internationally , intensified by global outrage over Gaza and wider regional escalation . Even governments traditionally aligned with Washington are becoming more cautious about unconditional @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ warfare is increasing . <p> Another significant factor is strategic resilience . Despite massive strikes on military and nuclear facilities , Iran has not collapsed internally . Predictions of regime implosion have once again proven exaggerated . <p> Instead , external attack often strengthens nationalist cohesion . History repeatedly shows that societies under siege tend to rally around sovereignty , even when internal dissent exists . Foreign military pressure can unintentionally consolidate rather than weaken ruling structures . <p> None of this means Iran is " winning " in any simplistic sense . Iran has suffered extensive damage . Civilian suffering remains profound . Israeli civilians have also faced missile attacks and insecurity . International humanitarian law must apply universally , whether violations are committed by Israel , Iran , or any other actor . <p> But strategically , Iran does not need battlefield domination to succeed . It only needs to prevent defeat . That is the lesson powerful states repeatedly fail to learn . <p> The deeper crisis exposed by this war is therefore not merely military . It is civilizational and geopolitical . The conflict reveals the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in a changing world . <p> The old order is fading . <p> The emerging world is more fragmented , multipolar , and resistant to unilateral power . Iran 's ability to withstand pressure from Israel and the United States -- despite enormous asymmetries -- illustrates that transformation vividly . <p> Whether one supports Iran or opposes its government is ultimately beside the point . This is not truth-telling ; it is a contribution to the subjugation of Muslim women by pre-emptively silencing the very reformers who are fighting for them . <p> Sharia vs . Fiqh : The Distinction That Dismantles Spencer 's Argument <p> Spencer writes that the Taliban are " ordering all of Afghan society according to Sharia , " treating this as if Sharia were a ready-made statutory code that one can simply " apply . " This displays a foundational ignorance of Islamic jurisprudence that would disqualify any academic submission . <p> Scholars distinguish sharply between Sharia -- the divine , abstract ethical ideal of justice and mercy toward which Islamic law aspires -- and Fiqh -- @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that attempts to approximate that ideal . Fiqh is not monolithic . The four Sunni schools ( Hanafi , Maliki , Shafi'i , and Hanbali ) and the Shia Jafari school have disagreed for centuries on nearly every significant legal question , including marriage , consent , and the rights of women in divorce . <p> The Taliban 's decree is a specific synthesis of the Deobandi school 's literalism overlaid with Pashtunwali tribal codes . It does not represent " the Sharia " ; it represents one hyper-patriarchal Fiqh -- a Fiqh that has been explicitly rejected by the Islamic Fiqh Academy of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation , by Al-Azhar University in Egypt ( which in 2019 issued a declaration supporting a minimum marriage age of eighteen ) , and by the jurisprudential consensus of the vast majority of Muslim-majority nations . Spencer 's refusal to acknowledge this centuries-old tradition of legal pluralism is not bold truth-telling ; it is a deliberate erasure of diversity designed to render Islam intellectually unreformable . <p> Spencer mocks the UN for " pretending that child marriage has nothing to do with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ does not claim that the Taliban 's language is non-Islamic ; it claims -- correctly -- that the Taliban 's interpretation is contested , minority , and condemned by mainstream Islamic scholarship . By maintaining this distinction , the UN performs an act of strategic intelligence , not diplomatic weakness . <p> Consider what would happen if the UN adopted Spencer 's framing and condemned Islam as a whole . The immediate consequence would be the destruction of every reformist Muslim women 's rights organisation operating in the Muslim world . Every activist who invokes the Quran 's concept of Karamah ( human dignity ) or the Prophet 's prohibition of compelled marriage would be handed over to the extremists who would declare , with Spencer 's implicit endorsement , that their religion itself is the enemy . The UN 's " precision " is not cowardice ; it is a lifeline to the women Spencer claims to care about . <p> What the Quran Actually Says <p> Spencer 's scriptural argument for the " Islamicity " of child marriage rests primarily on Surah Al-Talaq , verse 4 . He @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ those who have not menstruated " constitutes explicit permission for the marriage of pre-pubescent girls . <p> This reading fails at the first level of linguistic analysis . Throughout Surah Al-Talaq , the word used is Nisa -- a classical Arabic term designating adult women . The Hans Wehr Dictionary of Modern Written Arabic and the classical Lisan al-Arab both confirm that Nisa is the plural of mar'a ( a woman who has reached adulthood ) . The Quran uses entirely different vocabulary when speaking of children : Tifl ( singular ) and Atfal ( plural ) , as deployed in verses 22:5 and 24:59 . The Quran 's linguistic architecture is precise . If chapter 65 were intended to legislate for children , the word Atfal would have been used . The presence of Nisa is not incidental ; it is dispositive . <p> The verse addresses three categories of divorced adult women for whom calculating the waiting period ( Iddah ) is complex : post-menopausal women , women with amenorrhoea ( which affects adult women for hormonal , medical , and nutritional reasons ) , and pregnant women @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ licence for child marriage . <p> Spencer and the Taliban reduce the Islamic " age of marriage " to Bulugh -- physical puberty alone . They ignore the Quran 's decisive verse 4:6 , which establishes a two-tiered threshold for adult responsibility : first Bulugh ( physical maturity ) , and then Rushd ( sound judgment , intellectual and moral capacity ) . The verse links the " age of marriage " directly to demonstrable Rushd . If a person is not judged capable of managing their own property -- the immediate context of 4:6 -- they are , by Quranic logic , incapable of entering into what verse 4:21 calls a Mithaq Ghaliz -- a " solemn covenant . " <p> This term is weighty beyond measure . Mithaq Ghaliz is used elsewhere in the Quran only to describe the covenant between God and the Prophets -- the most sacred of divine bonds . A covenant , in any legal or spiritual sense , requires the capacity of the parties to understand and freely enter it . A nine-year-old , by any standard of human development , lacks the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and social implications of a lifelong union . The Taliban 's decree therefore does not enact an Islamic marriage ; it enacts what the Quran itself would recognise as a legal nullity -- a contract without genuine Ahliyyah ( legal capacity ) . <p> Perhaps the most decisive refutation of Spencer 's argument lies not in complex jurisprudence but in a foundational legal maxim attributed to the Prophet : " No harm shall be inflicted or reciprocated " ( La darar wa la dirar ) . This principle is not peripheral ; it is , alongside the Five Objectives of Islamic Law ( Maqasid al-Sharia ) , the backbone of Islamic ethical jurisprudence . <p> The medical and social scientific evidence is incontrovertible : child marriage causes severe physical harm ( obstetric fistula , maternal mortality , stunted development ) , profound psychological harm ( anxiety , depression , post-traumatic stress ) , and lifelong educational and economic deprivation . Under the principles of Usul al-Fiqh ( Islamic legal theory ) , any practice demonstrably causing this level of harm to a human being must be prohibited , regardless @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " deviation from Islam ; it is Islam 's own legal logic applied consistently . Spencer 's claim that the Taliban are enacting " authentic Islam " by perpetuating demonstrable , severe harm to children is , by the religion 's own internal standards , a theological absurdity . <p> De-Weaponising the Aisha Narrative <p> Spencer 's polemics consistently invoke the reported age of the Prophet Muhammad 's wife Aisha as the permanent normative standard for Islamic marriage law . He presents the traditional account -- six at betrothal , nine at consummation -- as an indisputable historical fact and an eternal divine template . <p> The historiographical case for a young Aisha rests on a narrow set of hadith that modern scholarship has subjected to rigorous historical-critical analysis . Dr Joshua Little 's doctoral research at the University of Oxford demonstrated that these age-reports emerged in the Iraqi hadith tradition over a century after the Prophet 's death , suggesting they are products of later memory-formation and possibly political contestation rather than contemporary eyewitness record . Alternative historiographical lines -- including calculations derived from the documented age of Aisha @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ her mid-to-late teens at the time of her marriage . <p> Even if one accepts the traditional account for the sake of argument , the inference Spencer draws is a non sequitur . In seventh-century Arabia , the transition from childhood to adulthood was tied to puberty across all cultures -- Christian , Jewish , pagan , and pre-Islamic Arab alike . Life expectancy was short ; the concept of extended childhood as a protected developmental phase is a product of modern education , medicine , and social organisation . The Quran does not set a numerical age ; it sets an ethical standard of Rushd . The Prophet 's actions were reformist and contextual within his time . To extract a specific historical event from a specific seventh-century context and apply it as an immutable divine command in a world with universal primary education , modern medicine , and international human rights law is what theologians call " hermeneutical violence " -- the weaponisation of text against its own ethical trajectory . <p> The Ideological Architecture of a Polemicist <p> To understand Spencer 's article , one must understand @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Watch , a blog that since 2003 has been classified by the Southern Poverty Law Center as a platform propagating anti-Muslim content . He is a Shillman Fellow at the David Horowitz Freedom Center -- a far-right ideological institution with a documented record of funding Islamophobic campaigns . He has written over thirty books with titles like The Politically Incorrect Guide to Islam and The Tragedy of Islam : Failure and Excuses ( 2026 ) . He was banned from the United Kingdom in 2013 as an extremist , and his writings were cited approvingly dozens of times in the manifesto written by Norwegian mass murderer Anders Breivik before the 2011 Oslo and Ut ? ya attacks that killed 77 people . Spencer has no academic credential in Islamic studies ; he holds a master 's degree in religious studies from the University of North Carolina , with no specialist training in Arabic , Islamic jurisprudence , or the historiography of the Muslim world . <p> This is not an ad hominem attack . It is necessary context for evaluating his claims . When Spencer calls the UN 's position @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ whose authority ? When he declares that the Taliban represent " authentic Islam , " we must ask : by what methodology ? The answer , across thirty-plus books , is always the same -- a method of selective citation , de-contextualised proof-texting , and the systematic silencing of the fourteen centuries of Islamic reformist thought that contradict his thesis . <p> Perhaps the most illuminating lens through which to understand Spencer 's worldview is not his writing on Islam but his writing on Israel and Palestine . Spencer is an ardent and documented supporter of Israeli military policy , including its most lethal expressions . After the October 7 , 2023 Hamas attack on Israel , Spencer 's platform doubled down on the position that any sympathy for Palestinian civilian suffering was equivalent to supporting terrorism . His book The Palestinian Delusion argues -- breathtakingly -- that the Palestinian people themselves are a " propaganda invention , " a claim so historically reckless that it erases the documented existence of centuries of Arab-Christian and Arab-Muslim communities on the land . He has consistently endorsed Israeli military operations in Gaza @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a population over half of whom were children . <p> The contradiction here is enormous and must be named clearly . Spencer devotes his professional life to condemning what he calls " the Islamic devaluation of human life . " Yet he is a vocal champion of a military campaign that , by the documented record of the UN , Medecins Sans Frontieres , and international human rights organisations , has killed tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians -- the vast majority of whom were neither fighters nor militants , but children , women , the elderly , and the sick . He rails against the Taliban killing girls by the mechanism of forced marriage ; he applauds -- or studiously ignores -- the killing of girls by the mechanism of aerial bombardment in Gaza . <p> This is not a political argument about the complexity of the Israel-Palestine conflict . It is a moral argument about consistency . A person who genuinely centres the protection of Muslim children as a moral absolute can not simultaneously wave away the deaths of Palestinian Muslim children as acceptable collateral damage in a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Spencer 's project ; it is definitional . His concern for Afghan girls is not compassion . It is a rhetorical instrument , deployed in the service of a broader civilisational argument whose conclusion is determined in advance : Islam is uniquely evil , and its people are uniquely dangerous . <p> There is a further dimension to this contradiction that demands frank acknowledgement . Spencer has argued , with extraordinary intellectual recklessness , that the Palestinian people are a modern " propaganda invention " -- that they did not exist as a people before the 1960s and that their national identity was constructed by Soviet intelligence operations . This claim erases centuries of documented Arab-Christian and Arab-Muslim community life in the Levant , the archives of Ottoman land records , the testimonies of Western travellers , and the scholarship of countless historians across multiple national traditions . To deny the historical existence and cultural continuity of a people in order to delegitimise their claims to rights and dignity is , ironically , precisely the kind of civilisational erasure Spencer claims to oppose when it is directed at Western cultures @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ operating logic of his entire enterprise . <p> When Spencer writes about Muslim girls under the Taliban , his prose becomes vivid with moral outrage . When Muslim girls die under other circumstances -- in the bombed hospitals of Gaza , in the refugee camps of Jordan , in the detention facilities on Europe 's borders -- his platform is largely silent , or worse , actively hostile to those calling attention to their suffering . The conclusion is unavoidable : Spencer 's humanitarianism is tribal , not universal . It is activated by suffering that can be attributed to Islam and deactivated by suffering that can not . This is not the architecture of human rights advocacy ; it is the architecture of ideological warfare . <p> What Spencer 's Christianity Demands of Him <p> Spencer claims to write from within the Catholic Christian tradition . This claim demands engagement , because the spirit of Jesus of Nazareth , whose teachings Spencer claims to honour , is in absolute and irreconcilable tension with everything Spencer 's platform represents . <p> Jesus did not identify the faith of a people @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Samaritan woman at the well ( John 4:1 -- 42 ) , he crossed every boundary of ethnic hatred and religious exclusion that his society enforced . The Samaritans were regarded by many first-century Jews with precisely the hostility that Spencer directs at Muslims -- as a corrupted , semi-heretical people whose practices were an affront to true faith . Jesus sat with her , spoke with her , recognised her humanity , and offered her his message . He did not first demand that she condemn her entire people 's theology . <p> When Jesus said " Love your enemies " ( Matthew 5:44 ) , he was not offering a sentimental platitude . He was issuing the most radical political challenge of the ancient world : refuse the logic of collective demonisation . The logic that says " because some among your people do evil , your entire people are irredeemable " is precisely the logic that Jesus consistently refused . The parable of the Good Samaritan ( Luke 10:25 -- 37 ) is , among other things , a direct refutation of ethnic and religious essentialism : @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ one from the despised tradition . <p> Slinging mud at 1.8 billion people -- attributing the specific crimes of a militant minority to an entire civilisation -- is , in the deepest sense , a betrayal of Jesus ' message . It is the spirit of those who came to stone the woman ( John 8:1 -- 11 ) , not the spirit of the one who drew in the sand and said " Let him who is without sin cast the first stone . " Spencer 's platform does not embody Christian civilisational defence ; it embodies a Christianity hollowed of its own most essential commandments -- the commandments of mercy , of solidarity with the persecuted , and of love for those whom one 's own tribe has declared the enemy . <p> The deep irony is this : The Jesus who is so casually invoked by counter-jihad Christianity as a symbol of Western civilisation would , by the logic of his own teachings , far more likely be found sitting with a Palestinian woman weeping over her bombed home in Rafah , or with an Afghan girl @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ less likely to be found writing polemical blog posts about the essential backwardness of their traditions . <p> A Call to Interreligious Solidarity <p> We arrive , finally , at what this paper insists is the only morally and intellectually honest response to the situation Spencer exploits : a genuine , rigorous , interreligious covenant of reform . <p> Let us be absolutely honest about something that Spencer 's polemical framing is designed to obscure : the subjugation of women in the name of God is not an Islamic invention . It is the shared shame of every major religious tradition in human history , and the recognition of this fact is the indispensable foundation of any genuine reform . <p> Christianity authorised centuries of witch-burning , enforced female silence in liturgy ( 1 Corinthians 14:34 -- 35 , a text whose Pauline authorship remains disputed ) , justified the legal subservience of wives under the doctrine of coverture , and provided theological cover for colonialism 's particular brutalisation of women of colour . The Catholic Church , to which Spencer belongs , spent centuries opposing women 's education , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has to this day not permitted women 's ordination . The Orthodox Jewish tradition developed the agunah system , which gives husbands the power to hold wives in a state of permanent legal limbo by refusing to grant a religious divorce . The Hindu tradition produced sati -- widow immolation -- and continues in many communities to enforce caste-based restrictions on women 's freedom that are enforced by violence . Buddhist monastic traditions across Asia have historically subordinated nuns to monks in ways that directly contradict the Buddha 's own egalitarian teachings . <p> This is not a competition in historical shame . It is a recognition that patriarchy is a human disease that has infected every religious vessel it has encountered , because religion , as a social institution wielding tremendous authority , has always been a prime vector for the legitimisation of power . The question is not " which tradition is uniquely patriarchal " -- they all have been . The question is : what does the authentic ethical core of each tradition demand of its adherents today ? <p> In every tradition , the reformers are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , Khaled Abou El Fadl , Tariq Ramadan , and Jasser Auda have constructed rigorous , textually grounded arguments for gender equity , minimum marriage ages , and women 's full legal personhood -- not by abandoning their faith , but by recovering its highest aspirations . In Judaism , the Reform and Conservative movements , along with feminist scholars like Rachel Adler , have transformed the legal status of women through Halacha itself . In Christianity , liberation theologians , feminist theologians like Elisabeth Schussler Fiorenza , and the ecumenical movement have recovered the radically egalitarian Jesus beneath centuries of patriarchal accretion . In Hinduism , reformers from Ram Mohan Roy to contemporary Dalit feminist activists have used the tradition 's own resources to resist its patriarchal deformations . <p> These reformers are the authentic voices of their traditions . They are not " pretenders , " as Spencer would have it of Muslim reformers . They are the people doing the hard , dangerous , necessary work of insisting that the sacred texts of humanity mean what they say when they speak of justice , mercy , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ this paper is simple , and it is addressed to people of every faith : reformation is not a betrayal of tradition -- it is tradition 's highest obligation . The great reformers in every tradition did not stand outside their scriptures and condemn them ; they stood inside them and recovered their highest aspirations against the patriarchal accretion of centuries . Martin Luther did not reject Christianity ; he insisted that it be read more honestly . B.R. Ambedkar did not simply leave Hinduism ; he called its highest ideals against its most degraded practices . The founders of Reform Judaism did not abandon Torah ; they insisted that its ethical core demanded evolution in its legal application . And the Muslim reformers -- from Muhammad Abduh to Amina Wadud to Jasser Auda -- do not abandon the Quran ; they insist that La darar ( no harm ) , Rushd ( maturity ) , and Rida ( consent ) mean exactly what they say . <p> For this reformation to be genuine and lasting , it must be interreligious . Muslim women fighting against child marriage in Afghanistan @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Manila are fighting the same battle against ecclesiastical patriarchy in their own communities . Jewish women seeking equal religious standing need solidarity from Muslim and Hindu women who understand the experience of being told that God 's law requires their subordination . Hindu women resisting caste-enforced marriage need the public support of communities across the world 's faiths . And none of these women need Robert Spencer purporting to speak for them while simultaneously denying the humanity of their Palestinian sisters . <p> The interreligious covenant this paper calls for is not the soft pluralism of vague spiritual solidarity . It is a hard , specific , textually-engaged commitment : to use the resources of each tradition against the patriarchal power structures that have corrupted it , to stand in solidarity across confessional lines with every reformer fighting that fight , and to refuse the polemicist 's gambit of weaponising women 's suffering in the service of civilisational war . <p> The enemy is not Islam . The enemy is not Christianity , Judaism , Hinduism , or Buddhism . The enemy is the patriarchal will to power that has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and used that authority to silence , diminish , and harm women for millennia . Every religion carries within it -- sometimes buried deep beneath centuries of patriarchal interpretation , but always recoverable -- a vision of the human person as inherently dignified , inherently deserving of freedom , inherently worthy of love and covenant rather than coercion . <p> The Taliban 's Decree No. 18 is a crime against that vision . So , by a different mechanism , is every system in every tradition that treats women as vessels for male authority rather than as full participants in the covenant of human community . <p> Robert Spencer 's commentary on the Taliban 's child marriage decree is not a defence of Afghan girls . It is a prosecution of their faith , conducted over their heads and against their expressed interests . It silences the Muslim women activists who are fighting Decree No. 18 using Quranic arguments . It hands the Taliban the ideological victory they most need : the assurance that the only alternative to their vision of Islam is the wholesale condemnation of their civilisation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Spencer invokes . And it perpetuates the moral double standard of a man who weeps for girls under Taliban rule while endorsing the military campaigns that have killed thousands of girls under other rubble . <p> The UN is not " absurd . " Its refusal to indict a global civilisation for the crimes of a militant faction is an act of both moral clarity and strategic intelligence . It is the position that respects the agency of the Muslim reformers who are the best -- and only -- hope for the Afghan girls Spencer exploits . <p> The authentic covenant of maturity insists on four things simultaneously : <p> First , that the Taliban 's decree is an abomination -- a violation of the Quranic ethic of Rushd , Rida , and Karamah , and a direct affront to the Prophet 's own teachings on women 's agency . <p> Second , that this abomination is the product of a specific political movement within a specific historical context , and says nothing definitive about the faith of 1.8 billion people . <p> Third , that every religious tradition has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ this shared legacy is an interreligious , not a competitive , project . <p> Fourth , that genuine compassion for the girls of Afghanistan -- and for all women whose suffering is instrumentalised by polemicists -- demands solidarity with the reformers inside Islam , not rhetorical solidarity with a narrative that condemns the reformers as heretics . <p> The paper of hate is hereby answered by the paper of justice . Not because Islam is above criticism -- no tradition is -- but because the criticism that truly liberates women begins in solidarity with the women themselves , in every tradition and against every patriarchy that dares to dress itself in the language of God . <h> Subscribe to Our Newsletter <p> V.A . @@137563480 <h> Blocked From Mecca -- How Gaza 's Siege Targets the Sacred <p> There is something profoundly barbaric about preventing a besieged people from reaching God . More than 10,000 Palestinians have been barred from undertaking the sacred journey to Mecca . <p> Elderly believers who waited decades for this moment now face the possibility of dying without fulfilling one of the central pillars of their faith . More than 70 selected pilgrims already have . This is not merely a restriction on movement . It is the deliberate humiliation of a people 's spiritual existence . They died waiting -- not because of fate alone , but because siege and war transformed worship into an impossibility . Some had saved for decades . Others waited years for their names to emerge through the official Hajj selection process . @@137595035 <h> The Exposed State : Israel , Gaza , and the Collapse of the Moral Architecture of the West <p> I was born in Laghouat , at the edge of the Algerian Sahara , in the house of Ahmed Chatta -- a man abducted by French colonial forces in 1958 and never seen again . No grave . No body . No official accounting . Only absence . <p> Colonial systems often erase in two stages . First the body disappears . Then the archive is organized around the disappearance . <p> I grew up inside that silence . <p> For that reason , when the first images from Gaza emerged after October 7 , 2023 , I recognized something immediately . Not the event itself . History never repeats itself mechanically . What I recognized was the grammar : the structure through which an entire population is progressively transformed into a demographic problem , a security burden , an obstacle to be managed , displaced , fragmented , or eliminated . <p> The vocabulary changes across centuries . The mechanism rarely does . <p> The destruction of civilian infrastructure @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The language of biological threat . The normalization of mass death . The bureaucratic management of starvation . The transformation of entire urban spaces into kill zones . <p> These are not accidental excesses appearing suddenly in wartime . They belong to a recognizable historical architecture . <p> This text is not written as a slogan , nor as an exercise in rhetorical outrage . It is written as a historical and legal record grounded in publicly documented evidence : United Nations investigations , rulings and provisional measures issued by the International Court of Justice , arrest warrants from the International Criminal Court , humanitarian reports , medical documentation , demographic data , journalistic investigations , and statements made publicly by Israeli officials themselves . <p> The purpose is not merely to denounce . It is to establish continuity between evidence , language , law , and power . <p> Future historians will not suffer from lack of documentation regarding Gaza . The quantity of archived material is already unprecedented . The question that will confront future generations is different : <p> How did the international system continue supplying weapons @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ accumulated in real time ? <p> DIFFERENTIAL HUMANITY <p> Israel presents itself internationally as " the Middle East 's only democracy . " The phrase has been repeated for decades by Western governments and media institutions as a self-evident truth requiring no serious examination . <p> Palestinians in the occupied territories remain subject to military orders , administrative detention , movement restrictions , land confiscation , permit regimes , military courts , and expanding settlement infrastructures considered illegal under international law . <p> This dual structure has been documented extensively by major human rights organizations long before October 2023 . <p> In 2021 , Human Rights Watch published A Threshold Crossed , concluding that Israeli authorities were committing the crimes against humanity of apartheid and persecution . <p> In 2022 , Amnesty International reached similar conclusions in its report Israel 's Apartheid Against Palestinians . <p> The Israeli human rights organization B'Tselem had already described the governing structure as " a regime of Jewish supremacy from the Jordan River to the Mediterranean Sea . It takes us back to Palestine between 1936 and 1939 , showing how the seeds of everything unfolding today in Palestine/Israel were sown during that very period by imperial Britain . <p> The film opens with beautiful depictions of thriving life in Palestinian villages and towns -- cotton fields , rivers , mountains , bustling coastal trade routes . The way director Annemarie Jacir brings this geography and the vibrant communal life inhabiting it onto the screen transforms the land itself into one of the film 's most important characters . But this portrayal is not accidental . Through it , Jacir demolishes the myth that Palestine was an empty , barren land upon which Jews arriving from Europe were settled and later " made fertile " through their labor . <p> Every @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and in this process , they endured much the same violence that Israel is inflicting upon Palestinians today . Perhaps for the first time , this film portrays that revolt with both beauty and political commitment . By incorporating contemporary newsreel footage throughout , the director firmly anchors the film in historical authenticity . <p> At the beginning of the film , we are introduced to its central character , Yusuf , who has arrived in the city in search of work . @@137626658 <h> The Promise and Failure of International Law <p> The International Court of Justice ( ICJ ) was created on a pretty straightforward idea : even after the devastating impact of the biggest war in human history , countries could be persuaded to settle their disputes in a courtroom rather than resorting to violence . While the founders of this post-1945 world did n't think every power would bend to the rule of law , they felt that with a well-structured institution , the path to war could at least be made less automatic . The ICJ was established in 1945 as the main judicial branch of the United Nations , with the hope that it would serve this purpose . <p> Fast forward nearly eighty years , and that initial hope seems more uncertain than ever . <p> That does n't mean the ICJ has been completely ineffective . For countries that do n't have the military strength to resolve conflicts , even a legal ruling can carry significant weight . It can help them gain leverage , change the diplomatic landscape , and ramp up pressure on the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ interpretations , and issues around diplomatic immunity , the ICJ has indeed made a difference . The challenge arises when the stakes are much higher . <p> When Big Powers Get Involved <p> One of the biggest limitations of the International Court of Justice is that it has no real power to enforce its rulings . It can not arrest leaders , impose sanctions , or force countries to comply . In practice , its authority depends largely on whether states are willing to follow international law . When powerful countries refuse , accountability often stalls at the UN Security Council , where veto powers shield allies and weaken enforcement . <p> This exposes a deeper contradiction within the international legal system : it works best when political stakes are low , but struggles when major powers are involved . <p> The clearest recent example is South Africa 's genocide case against Israel under the Genocide Convention . The ICJ issued binding provisional measures -- legal orders , not mere suggestions -- calling for steps to prevent further harm in Gaza . Yet the violence continued , and much of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cases , powerful states actively shielded Israel from consequences , even as Gaza faced catastrophic humanitarian destruction . <p> The reality is stark . The court issued firm directives , but there was little meaningful enforcement . <p> A year after the UN General Assembly backed the ICJ 's advisory opinion declaring Israel 's occupation of Palestinian territories illegal , many states still had not taken concrete action . UN experts warned that this reflected a serious decline in the credibility of the multilateral system . By then , hundreds of thousands of Palestinians had been killed or injured , millions faced starvation , and nearly the entire population of Gaza had been displaced , often repeatedly . <p> Undermining Justice <p> While the ICJ and the International Criminal Court ( ICC ) serve different purposes -- the ICJ settles disputes between countries while the ICC holds individuals accountable for serious international crimes -- the situation with the ICC in the past year has highlighted how far powerful nations will go to protect themselves and their allies from being held accountable . <p> On February 6 , 2025 , President @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sanctions on anyone attempting to engage the ICC in investigations or prosecutions concerning U.S. officials or those from allied countries . Following this , there was a systematic effort to sanction individuals . By December 18 , 2025 , eleven ICC prosecutors and judges had been sanctioned , including the chief prosecutor , two deputy prosecutors , and eight judges . <p> These were n't people accused of wrongdoing . The ICC had issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister due to alleged war crimes . Secretary of State Marco Rubio labelled the court a ' national security threat ' and an ' instrument of lawfare ' against both the U.S. and Israel . <p> So a court that investigates war crimes is considered a threat to national security ? As a result , judges who are merely doing their jobs are placed under sanctions . Even Francesca Albanese , a UN expert on Palestine , faced sanctions just for producing reports . A UN expert noted that these actions strike at the very heart of international justice , the promise that no @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that the United States and Israel are not party to the Rome Statute , a decision not taken lightly . By choosing not to join , they effectively shield themselves from accountability , and they can impose sanctions on anyone who tries to challenge that . <p> Selective Universality <p> This pattern is n't new . While international law is supposed to apply universally , it often only does so selectively . When a less powerful state is accused , the court 's decisions can have real consequences . But when a state has backing from a powerful ally , the court 's influence seems to vanish once it meets political calculations . <p> This selectivity is n't just a flaw in ethics ; it 's a fundamental issue . A court ca n't serve as a fair referee in a system where power is so unevenly distributed . The founding principles of the ICJ assumed mutual respect among nations , which has rarely been present . @@137626679 <h> When Physicians Write the Nation : Rizal and the Ethics of Speaking Beyond the Body <p> A physician ends a long day in the clinic -- listening , examining , absorbing -- and then , instead of stopping , begins to write . Not prescriptions or charts , but sentences that try to make sense of what medicine alone can not fix . For some , this crossing of boundaries feels uncomfortable . The doctor , in this view , should remain within the body : technical , precise , contained . <p> But the deeper question is not why some physicians write . <p> It is why others are expected not to . <p> To practice medicine is to stand , daily , at the intersection of biology and circumstance . Illness rarely arrives alone . It carries the weight of poverty , the imprint of violence , the erosion of dignity . A doctor who treats disease without seeing the conditions that produce it risks practicing a thinner form of care -- one that heals , but does not fully understand . <p> Few lives illuminate this @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Born under Spanish colonial rule in the Philippines , Rizal trained as an ophthalmologist in Madrid , Paris , and Heidelberg . His early ambition was intimate and precise : to restore his mother 's sight . But what he encountered abroad -- and what he came to understand about his own country -- shifted that purpose . The deeper blindness , he realized , was not ocular . <p> It was political . Cultural . Structural . <p> When he returned home , he could have confined himself to clinical work . Instead , he began to write . His novels , Noli Me Tangere and El Filibusterismo , did not merely tell stories ; they exposed a system . They traced how power -- colonial , clerical , and social -- shaped what people could see , say , and become . <p> Rizal did not simply write about a nation . <p> He helped write it into existence . <p> He did not call for violence . He called for recognition -- for the radical act of seeing clearly . That alone made him dangerous . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ they silenced in the moment , they amplified in history . His words outlived him , helping to form a national consciousness that no decree could contain . <p> Rizal is remembered as a writer , a martyr , a national hero . But at his core , he remained a physician : observant , methodical , attentive to suffering . What changed was not his method , but the scale at which he applied it . He expanded the clinical gaze -- from the individual body to the body politic . <p> That expansion remains uneasy even today . <p> There are valid concerns about physicians entering public discourse . Medical authority does not automatically confer political wisdom . In polarized societies , advocacy can be misread as partisanship ; trust , once strained , is difficult to restore . <p> And yet , the realities of contemporary medicine make silence increasingly difficult to justify . <p> In Gaza , Sudan , and Ukraine , physicians have documented patterns of injury that point to systematic harm rather than isolated events . Organizations such as M ? decins Sans Fronti @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on hospitals and healthcare workers . The World Health Organization has reported hundreds of such incidents in a single year . These are not abstract policy debates . They are clinical observations with moral implications . <p> To witness such patterns and say nothing is not neutrality . <p> It is a narrowing of responsibility . <p> Rizal 's legacy does not demand that every physician become a novelist or a public intellectual . It asks something subtler : that medicine recognize its own boundaries -- and refuse to be confined by them when human suffering clearly exceeds those limits . <p> Across eras and continents , many physicians have done exactly that . They have documented torture when others denied it , warned of the medical consequences of nuclear war , reframed climate change as a matter of survival , and helped build the ethical and legal frameworks that protect civilians in conflict . @@137644798 <h> Opinion India 's West Asia challenge : Stay agile , stay connected <h> Rarely in recent years has West Asia occupied so much space in India 's foreign-policy conversation . Attention , however , has not always produced understanding . By breakfast , newspaper columns have sorted the heroes and villains . By prime time , TV hosts have turned the crisis into loyalty tests . For India , West Asia is not a straight line . It is ... <p> For India , West Asia is not a straight line . It is a Rubik 's Cube . Every move shifts another face . ( Illustration : C R Sasikumar/File ) <p> Rarely in recent years has West Asia occupied so much space in India 's foreign-policy conversation . Attention , however , has not always produced understanding . By breakfast , newspaper columns have sorted the heroes and villains . By prime time , TV hosts have turned the crisis into loyalty tests . <p> For India , West Asia is not a straight line . It is a Rubik 's Cube . Every move shifts another @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Delhi to align with . Israel , the Gulf and Iran are three principal faces of the same puzzle . A posture that protects defence ties with Israel may complicate Gulf sensitivities . A channel that preserves access to Iran may unsettle partners elsewhere . <p> Advertisement <p> The first is a security and technology-oriented West Asia . Here , Israel matters . The relationship is embedded in defence procurement , intelligence-sharing and counter-terrorism capabilities . In a crisis , these are operational assets . Any serious Indian policy must account for this layer , however uncomfortable that may be for those who prefer a purely moral frame . <p> The second is an economic and human West Asia , the Gulf . For India , it means remittances , oil , gas , investment flows , food security and the safety of its workers abroad . Saudi Arabia and the UAE are both indispensable , but they are not interchangeable . Riyadh carries the weight of oil markets , Islamic legitimacy and bargaining in any future regional settlement . Inside , I saw his three sons eating , but the atmosphere was subdued and heavy . <p> The joy that should have filled the air was missing . And it was n't just that one house -- this quiet unease now hangs over the entire country . Festivals , once occasions of celebration , now bring more anxiety than happiness . It is the systematic dismantling of a people , their history , and their right to exist on their own land . Every hospital bombed , every school flattened , every starving child trapped beneath rubble exposes a brutal truth : this is not about " security . " It is about domination , occupation , and control . <p> Israel 's actions in Gaza have crossed every moral and legal boundary recognised by humanity . Entire neighbourhoods have been erased from the map . Civilians are denied food , medicine , water , and electricity . Aid convoys are obstructed while desperate families are forced to survive in conditions unfit for human life . The language of " self-defence " has become a shield behind which collective punishment is inflicted upon more than two million Palestinians . <p> According to humanitarian agencies and UN estimates , tens of thousands of Palestinians have been killed in Gaza , the overwhelming majority of them civilians , including thousands of women and children . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and civilian infrastructure have reportedly been damaged or destroyed , while hundreds of thousands face famine-like conditions due to blockade and bombardment . Generations are being traumatised in real time . These are not accidental outcomes of war ; they reflect the deliberate scale of devastation inflicted upon an already besieged population . <p> The humanitarian catastrophe unfolding in Gaza has few parallels in recent history . Doctors are performing surgeries without anaesthesia . Families queue for hours for a piece of bread or a bucket of unsafe water . Children who survive bombings are growing up orphaned , displaced , and psychologically scarred . Journalists , aid workers , and medical personnel -- people protected under international law -- have themselves become targets of attack . What is being destroyed is not only infrastructure , but the social and moral fabric necessary for human survival . <p> But Gaza is not Israel 's land to seize . <p> The Palestinians are not foreigners in Gaza .
